sentence: Sertraline is an antidepressant from a group called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs.
note: NHS page classes sertraline as an SSRI antidepressant.

sentence: The NHS says it treats depression, obsessive compulsive disorder, panic disorder, post-traumatic stress disorder and social anxiety disorder.
note: NHS search summary listed these five conditions.

sentence: US information also mentions premenstrual dysphoric disorder.
note: Search summary said MedlinePlus mentions PMDD as a use; consistent with existing entry.

sentence: It is also used for obsessive compulsive disorder in children, and sometimes for severe depression in teenagers.
note: Search summary of NHS page: used for OCD in children aged 6 to 17 and sometimes severe depression in 12 to 17 (ages omitted).

sentence: It comes as tablets, and as a liquid concentrate that is diluted before use.
note: UK leaflets returned: tablets, and oral concentrate that must be diluted before use.

sentence: The NHS says sertraline is thought to work by raising the level of serotonin, a chemical in the brain linked to mood.
note: NHS summary: thought to work by increasing serotonin.

sentence: The NHS antidepressants overview says it is not known exactly how antidepressants work.
note: Overview page: not known exactly how they work; thought to increase neurotransmitters.

sentence: SSRIs are thought to block the reabsorption of serotonin, so more stays available to pass messages between nerve cells.
note: NHS 111 Wales SSRI page, as summarised by the search; not the main NHS page.

sentence: You may start to feel better within a week or two, but it usually takes several weeks to work fully.
note: One NHS page: feel better after 1 to 2 weeks, full effect after 4 to 6 weeks (numbers omitted).

sentence: The NHS lists headaches, feeling sick, dizziness or drowsiness, dry mouth, diarrhoea, sleep problems and reduced sex drive as common side effects.
note: NHS side effects page, as summarised.

sentence: Most side effects ease after a couple of weeks, as your body gets used to the medicine.
note: NHS: most side effects should ease after a couple of weeks.

sentence: The NHS advises against driving, cycling or using machinery while you feel dizzy or drowsy.
note: NHS: do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until symptoms pass.

sentence: Serious reactions are rare.
note: NHS side effects summary.

sentence: Serotonin syndrome is a rare but serious reaction, with confusion, agitation, fever, muscle stiffness and a fast heartbeat.
note: NHS-linked source in search, and antidepressants page flags serotonin syndrome as uncommon but potentially serious.

sentence: Some people may become unusually high or overactive, which doctors call hypomania or mania.
note: Antidepressants page: some people may experience hypomania or mania.

sentence: Low sodium in the blood is described as a rare but serious effect of SSRIs.
note: Case report in the NCBI results describing sertraline-related low sodium (hyponatraemia) as rare but serious.

sentence: MedlinePlus warns that sertraline may raise the risk of suicidal thoughts and actions in children, teenagers and young adults, especially early on and when the dose is increased.
note: MedlinePlus boxed warning, as summarised in the search.

sentence: If you have thoughts of suicide or self-harm and are in immediate danger, call 999; for urgent help call NHS 111 and choose the mental health option, or call Samaritans free on 116 123 at any time, and tell your GP at a routine review.
note: Crisis route from the site's existing sertraline entry and editorial policy; the searches returned only MedlinePlus advice to contact a doctor urgently, so this sentence is textbook.

sentence: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol while taking sertraline, because it can stop the medicine working properly.
note: NHS summary.

sentence: MedlinePlus adds that alcohol can make the side effects worse.
note: MedlinePlus, as summarised.

sentence: Grapefruit juice is advised against, because it may raise the amount of sertraline in the body.
note: NHS and UK leaflets, as summarised.

sentence: The NHS advises against using the herbal remedy St John's wort with sertraline.
note: NHS, as summarised.

sentence: MedlinePlus names tryptophan, aspirin, and anti-inflammatory painkillers such as ibuprofen and naproxen as possible interactions.
note: MedlinePlus, as summarised.

sentence: UK leaflets warn about blood thinners such as warfarin, and about medicines that affect heart rhythm, such as some antipsychotics and antibiotics.
note: UK leaflets, as summarised.

sentence: The leaflets also say sertraline must not be used with a group of antidepressants called MAOIs.
note: Leaflets list MAOI use as a contraindication.

sentence: Case reports describe serotonin syndrome when sertraline was combined with cough medicine containing dextromethorphan, or with herbal supplements.
note: NCBI case report: Bromfed DM with sertraline; other reports mention unregulated supplements.

sentence: UK leaflets say to tell the doctor or pharmacist about every medicine you take, including herbal ones.
note: Leaflets, as summarised.

sentence: The NHS says most adults can take sertraline.
note: NHS summary.

sentence: It may not suit people with diabetes, epilepsy, heart disease, glaucoma, a bleeding disorder or a past episode of mania.
note: NHS summary of who cannot take it / needs checks.

sentence: Anyone allergic to sertraline or its ingredients should not take it.
note: Leaflets list allergy as a contraindication.

sentence: UK leaflets say people under 18 face a higher risk of effects such as suicide attempts and thoughts of self-harm.
note: Leaflet wording as summarised; adults under 25 also flagged for caution in one leaflet.

sentence: The NHS says sertraline can be taken in pregnancy.
note: NHS pregnancy page.

sentence: Some studies suggest it might occasionally affect a baby's heart development.
note: NHS pregnancy page.

sentence: Use in the last weeks can cause short-term withdrawal symptoms in the baby and, very rarely, breathing problems.
note: NHS pregnancy page.

sentence: Doctors should be told if you become pregnant.
note: Search summary of NHS page.

sentence: Sertraline can often be used while breastfeeding, but it passes into breast milk in small amounts, so it is best to check.
note: NHS pregnancy and breastfeeding page.

sentence: The NHS says not to stop suddenly, because this may cause withdrawal symptoms.
note: NHS sertraline and stopping pages.

sentence: Your doctor will usually reduce the amount gradually over several weeks or months.
note: NHS: gradual reduction over several weeks or months.

sentence: Withdrawal symptoms usually begin within days and generally last a week or two.
note: NHS stopping page: within 5 days, last 1 to 2 weeks (numbers omitted).

sentence: Some people have none, while others have severe symptoms that last for months or more.
note: NHS stopping page; antidepressants page says some may get none at all.

sentence: The Royal College of Psychiatrists says symptoms can start days or even weeks after a reduction.
note: RCPsych stopping page.

sentence: It adds that the gap between reductions should last as long as it takes symptoms to ease.
note: RCPsych stopping page.

sentence: The NHS advises seeing a doctor about severe symptoms, and options include slowing the reduction.
note: NHS stopping page: see doctor if severe; slower reduction among options.

sentence: Other options include going back to a medicine from the same group before reducing again.
note: NHS stopping page: reintroducing another antidepressant from the same group.

sentence: The NHS says you may start to feel better within a week or two, but it usually takes several weeks to work fully.
note: As above.

sentence: Side effects often come first and tend to ease after a couple of weeks.
note: NHS summary.

sentence: Early on, some people feel more anxious before they feel better.
note: Existing entry cites NHS that anxiety can be worse before better; search did not return it directly, so lower confidence.

sentence: MedlinePlus says people are advised to keep taking it even when they feel well.
note: MedlinePlus, as summarised.

sentence: The NHS says antidepressants are usually taken for a good while after you feel better.
note: NHS summary: at least some months after symptoms improve (number omitted).

sentence: Stopping is done gradually with your doctor.
note: NHS.

sentence: A plan to reduce the amount is usually agreed over several weeks or months.
note: NHS.

note: NHS.

sentence: Some studies suggest a possible effect on a baby's heart development, though this is described as occasional.
note: NHS.

note: NHS pregnancy page.
